To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a 2-week exposure to non-traumatic noise opens a critical period for plasticity in the rat auditory cortex, and that this plasticity can be maladaptive, leading to hyperacusis but no tinnitus.
we have demonstrated that a 2-week exposure to non-traumatic noise opens windows of plasticity for reorganization in the central auditory system.

we have demonstrated, for the first time, that passive sound exposure leads to hyperacusis in rats, and we have shown that this hyperacusis is accompanied by a functional reorganization in the central auditory system that is associated with an improvement in the sensorimotor gating function of the acoustic startles response.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the auditory system in the generation of hyperacusis and tinnitus.
the question of how the brain adapts to changes in its environment and how this adaptation may be influenced by the presence of hearing disorders.
understanding how the brain changes in response to auditory experience and how these changes may contribute to the development of hearing disorders.

noise exposure can induce hyperacusis, but it does not induce tinnitus.
noise-induced plasticity in the auditory system is not a necessary and sufficient condition for the development of hyperacusis or tinnitus.

the auditory system has the ability to reorganize in response to environmental changes.
